title: The Suspicious Email
briefing: An employee at Northbridge Fictional Corp reported receiving an urgent email asking them to verify their account credentials through an external link.
learning_objectives: Inspect sender details, links, and urgency cues in a simulated phishing email
Distinguish relevant investigation evidence from non-relevant items
Choose a safe incident response action and explain why it matters

evidence.title: Reported Account Verification Email
evidence.content:
From: Security Desk <support@northbridge-verify.example.test>
To: jordan.patel@northbridge.example.test
Subject: Urgent: Password Reset Required Within 1 Hour
Body: Your account will be locked unless you sign in at http://northbridge-verify.example.test/login

evidence.title: Office Supply Order Note
evidence.content: Reminder: Extra dry-erase markers and sticky notes were delivered to the third-floor supply closet.

decisions.prompt: How should the employee handle the suspicious account-verification email?
options: Click the link and enter current login details to prevent account lock
Do not click the link and report the email to the security/IT team
Reply to the sender asking if the email is legitimate
decisions.feedback_correct: Reporting the suspicious email without clicking the link helps prevent credential theft and lets defenders investigate safely.
decisions.feedback_incorrect: Clicking links, replying to untrusted senders, or entering credentials in urgent messages can expose accounts to phishing.

hints.text: Start by looking for artificial urgency and unexpected requests to verify credentials.
Focus on the email and email header evidence rather than unrelated office notes.
Compare the sender/link domain against the company domain and check the SPF result.
Phishing uses social engineering—such as urgency and deceptive links—to trick users into giving up credentials.

conclusion.prompt: Summarize why this email is a phishing attempt and what action should be taken.
